passages.heading: The core idea
passages.markdown: A virtual machine presents virtual hardware to a guest operating system. The physical host supplies CPU time, RAM, storage, and networking through a hypervisor. A type 1 hypervisor runs directly on hardware, while a type 2 hypervisor runs on a host operating system. Both approaches need enough physical resources for their workloads; assigning more virtual memory than a host can support does not create real memory.

passages.heading: In the real world
passages.markdown: Virtual machines are useful for isolated test environments, legacy applications, and running different operating systems on one machine. Isolation is a design boundary, not a promise of perfect security. Patch guests and hypervisors, control shared folders, and choose network access deliberately. A snapshot captures a point-in-time state useful for rollback but is not an independent backup strategy. Containers typically share a host kernel instead of providing each workload a full guest kernel, so application packaging and virtual machines solve related but different problems.

passages.heading: Make it stick
passages.markdown: Put it into practice by explaining the decision in your own words. In a support scenario, identify the requirement first, connect it to the relevant technology, and check the result against that requirement. If the evidence changes, revisit your reasoning rather than repeating the same action. Document what you observed so the next person can understand your conclusion.
